questions.passage:
Keeping a record of colour

Textile researchers in a university collection wanted to compare how dyed fabrics changed after display. The team had earlier photographed each piece for cataloguing, but those photographs were made under different lamps. In some pictures a blue cloth appeared almost grey. The team decided that images would still be useful if the conditions for taking them were controlled.

Before each new photograph, staff positioned a colour chart beside the cloth. Its patches had known colours and provided a reference when staff compared images. Rather than mark the fabric to identify the area to photograph, staff recorded the position on a paper template. This meant they could find the same area on the next visit without putting ink or a pin through the textile.

Staff also recorded the number of display hours alongside each image. Two objects could have been on the exhibition list for the same number of weeks but have spent different amounts of time under the lights. Some were covered during teaching demonstrations and some remained uncovered.

For a small pilot, the team chose reproduction swatches to check whether repeated photographs taken by different staff members were consistent. This allowed the method to be adjusted before work began on the collection. The project team stressed that a visual change in successive images was evidence to investigate, and that a comparison photograph could not establish the chemical cause of a change.

Summary: Standardising the image collection

The original images varied because the pieces had been photographed under different [1] ___. For new images a [2] ___ provided patches of known colour. To locate an area again without marking the fabric, staff used a [3] ___. Alongside each image they entered the number of [4] ___, since time spent on the exhibition list could be misleading. Initial consistency checks used [5] ___ before the method was applied to the collection.

questions.passage:
Making a seed archive easier to search

A university garden receives seed donations from local growers. For many years its small collection could be searched by asking the manager, who recognised most of the envelopes. As the collection grew, the number of informal names also increased. A working group introduced a procedure to keep the names people supplied while making the collection searchable by staff who had never met the donors.

At intake, an assistant first records the donor name and the collection date on an intake sheet. The assistant then copies the writing on the original envelope exactly as it appears. This preserves spellings and local names even when the assistant cannot identify the plant immediately. Every donation receives an accession number, which allows staff to trace a new record to the correct envelope.

A curator then checks whether the supplied name can be linked confidently to a name in the reference list. If it cannot, the record is sent to a review queue for further investigation. Confident matches may go straight to the next stage. The original wording is retained in both cases.

Once a match has been confirmed, a searchable record is created. The sample is then stored in a cool cabinet alongside other material with the same storage requirements. Later researchers can use the record to trace the sample and compare its storage location with the latest inventory.

↓

↓
Once a match is confirmed, create the searchable record and store the sample in a [5] ___.
